turns.doctor_question: Did anything major happen in your life around the time this started?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yeah. I mean, I guess you could definitely say that. It wasn't just a single event like a car crash or a bad day on a detail, it was... it was a whole shift in my reality. 

My wife and I, we got divorced. And, you know, marriages in my line of work, they take a massive beating to begin with. You're never home, your schedule is dictated by the needs of the protectee, you miss anniversaries, birthdays... you name it. So, I'm not saying it was a total shock that it ended, but it still upends your whole life. I had to move out of our house—the house we bought together, the place where I had my routine, my garage, my gear room where I kept everything perfectly organized. 

I ended up having to move into this much smaller rental place. Just this cramped little apartment. And honestly, that's exactly when things really started unraveling. I can trace it right back to that specific transition. It was about a year and two months ago. Yeah, fourteen months. 

I remember the first week in that rental. I had all these cardboard boxes stacked up in the living room, and I just... I couldn't unpack them. I'd come home from a shift, walk through the door of this place that didn't even feel like mine, and I'd just sit on the couch staring at the boxes. I kept telling myself, "Alright, you're just adjusting. You're adapting to a new environment, assessing the new baseline, it takes time." Because that's what you do on the job, right? You adapt. But I never did. I just sat there. The walls felt like they were closing in, but at the exact same time, I just couldn't bring myself to care. 

I haven't even unpacked half of those boxes to this day. They're just sitting there, gathering dust, because the energy it takes to open them and find a place for my things just feels completely insurmountable. So, yeah, the divorce, and moving into that smaller rental a year and two months ago... that was the catalyst. That's when the thread really started pulling loose, and I just haven't been able to stop it from unraveling since.

turns.doctor_question: Has this low mood and shutdown been present most days for at least two years without a break?
turns.patient_response:
Two years? No, no, it hasn't been that long. I mean, I know sometimes when you're in the thick of it, time gets a little warped, right? Like when you're on a 48-hour watch and the second night feels like it stretches on for an entire decade, or when you're just staring at a wall and you lose track of whether it's Tuesday or Thursday. But no, I keep a very strict mental timeline of things. It's a deeply ingrained habit from the job—logging everything, keeping track of exact dates, times, shift changes. You never lose your sense of chronology when you're trained like I am. 

So I can tell you definitively that it hasn't been two years. Like I was just saying a minute ago, things really started unraveling since I moved into that smaller rental after my divorce. That is the exact starting line for all of this. That was about a year and two months ago. Fourteen months. 

Before that fourteen-month mark, even with the marriage falling apart and the lawyers and the arguments, I was still functioning at a hundred percent. I was still hitting the gym at zero-four-hundred, maintaining my gear, running my details without a single hitch. I was still me. The shutdown... this complete and total blankness... that didn't hit until I was actually in that new apartment, sitting on that couch, staring at those taped-up cardboard boxes. 

So, has it been most days since then? Yeah. Honestly, it's been every single day without a break since that move. It is a constant, heavy weight. But the actual timeline is a year and two months, not two years. It just feels like an absolute eternity when you're trapped inside it, you know what I mean? But chronologically, on paper, it's fourteen months.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient confirms experiencing a 'constant, heavy weight' and a 'shutdown' characterized by 'complete and total blankness' every single day for the past fourteen months.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been losing interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah. Yeah, that’s... honestly, that’s really the core of it right there. Mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore. I mean, if you look at my background, the way I've lived my whole life, I’ve always been an active guy. A doer. If I had downtime, I was filling it. But now... it’s like the engine is just completely flooded and won't turn over. 

I used to go hiking all the time. I had all my routes mapped out, I’d pack my rucksack, get out into the elevation just to clear my head and push my cardio, keep myself in top shape for the job. I haven't been on a trail in... well, since the move. My boots are just sitting in the closet. And coaching—I used to coach, too. Helping out, teaching teamwork, discipline, running drills. I just stopped showing up for it. I think I sent one brief text saying I was stepping back, and that was it. I didn't even care that I was leaving them hanging, which is so incredibly unlike me. My whole life is built on reliability, and I just dropped it.

Even the small stuff, the stuff I did just for me. I’ve played guitar since I was getting my bachelor's degree, just picking at an acoustic on the couch to decompress after a high-stress detail. Now? I don't even know if it's in tune. It's sitting in its case in the corner of the living room, and I have absolutely zero desire to open it. I don't even call people back anymore. My phone will vibrate, I'll look at the screen, see it's a buddy from a past detail or a family member, and I just watch it ring out. I tell myself I'll call them tomorrow, but tomorrow comes and I just stare at the phone again. 

And it’s not just that I don’t enjoy those things anymore, it’s like... the starter motor in my brain is just broken. Some days, I just sit in that small rental, right there on the couch next to those unpacked boxes I was telling you about, and I will literally sit there for hours. Just hours ticking by. The sun goes down, the room gets dark, and I’m just staring. I know there are things to do. I have a mental checklist—do the laundry, pay the electric bill, unpack the kitchen stuff, maybe just make a meal—and I know exactly how to do them, but I just... I can't make myself start. The physical act of standing up and initiating a single task feels like trying to deadlift a two-ton vehicle. It's just this heavy, paralyzing blankness.

turns.doctor_question: Have you started, stopped, or changed any alcohol or drug use around the time this began?
turns.patient_response:
Well... no. Honestly, people always ask that, especially given my line of work. You know, protective services... it's a culture that practically runs on black coffee and bourbon, right? Guys get off a high-stress detail, they hit the bar, they blow off steam. And you'd think, given everything I just told you—the divorce, moving into that cramped little rental fourteen months ago, just sitting there staring at those taped-up cardboard boxes until the room gets completely dark—you'd think I'd be hitting the bottle pretty hard. It would make perfect sense, wouldn't it? To try and numb it all out, or at least try to get a break from the blankness.

But no, I haven't started drinking, or using drugs, or anything like that. I haven't stopped either, because I was never really a heavy drinker to begin with. I mean, back before all this, I’d have a beer at a buddy's barbecue, or maybe a single glass of scotch if the team was celebrating the end of a long-term assignment, but that was really the extent of it. I've always had to stay sharp, stay ready for the next call, so I never messed around with anything that would compromise my reaction time. 

And since this whole shutdown started a year and two months ago, I haven't even had the desire to drink. Like I was saying about the guitar, or my hiking boots just sitting in the closet, the starter motor is completely broken. Even the idea of going down to the liquor store, picking out a six-pack, bringing it home, opening a bottle... it all just feels like way too much effort. It's insurmountable. I don't even have the energy to self-medicate, if that makes sense. I just sit there on the couch. So, no, there hasn't been any change in alcohol or drugs at all. It's definitely not a substance thing. It's just... exactly what I was describing before. Just that heavy, paralyzing weight.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever been diagnosed with a neurologic or medical condition such as Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, a brain tumor, or another chronic illness?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, nothing like that. No Parkinson’s, no MS, definitely no brain tumors or anything chronic. I mean, if you think about it, in my line of work—protective services—you absolutely cannot have anything like that on your record. They run you through the absolute wringer before they ever let you near a principal or put you on a high-stakes detail. I’m talking exhaustive annual physicals... EKGs, full blood panels, reflex tests, neurological workups, the whole nine yards. If I had a neurological issue or a tumor, the department docs would have flagged it years ago. 

I've always had a completely clean bill of health. In fact, right before the divorce really hit its peak, my physical showed I had the resting heart rate of a marathon runner. I took pride in that, you know? I kept this machine running perfectly. Aside from maybe some lower back stiffness from standing post in full gear for twelve hours straight on concrete, structurally and medically, I’m completely fine. No doctor has ever told me I have a chronic medical disease. 

And I guess... I guess that’s what makes this whole situation so incredibly frustrating. Because when I’m sitting there on that couch in the rental, staring at those same taped-up cardboard boxes as the sun goes down, my body feels like it weighs a thousand pounds. It feels like I *should* have some kind of severe physical illness, like my nerves just won't fire. You’d almost think it was something like MS with how physically impossible it feels to just stand up and walk to the kitchen to make a sandwich. But it's not. On paper, medically speaking, I am one hundred percent fit for duty. I've never been diagnosed with a single chronic medical issue in my entire life. It's just... whatever this heavy blankness is. But to answer your question, no, no tumors, no Parkinson's. Just a perfectly healthy body that I can't seem to operate anymore.

And like I was saying before about the department medical clearances... if I had taken a hit to the head, they would have run me through strict concussion protocols, scans, the whole battery of tests, and they would have benched me until I was one hundred percent cleared. But my file is absolutely spotless. No car accidents where I hit the steering wheel, no slipping on the ice and hitting the pavement, no getting clocked on a detail... nothing. 

So physically, structurally, my head hasn't taken any damage at all. It hasn't been injured. Which just brings me right back to sitting on that couch, you know?
